Getting started with suest

Source: vignettes/suest.Rmd
suest.Rmd

suest() combines two or more separately fitted models so you can test whether predictions, marginal effects, or other quantities differ across the models. It supplies the joint robust covariance matrix those tests need, and leaves calculating and presenting the quantities themselves to marginaleffects.

Functions at a glance

  • suest() combines two or more fitted models and calculates their joint covariance matrix.
  • suest_newdata() stacks the models’ estimation samples so each model’s effects can be averaged over its own sample.
  • suest_mi() pools suest() results across multiply imputed datasets.
  • The usual marginaleffects functions, including predictions(), avg_comparisons(), avg_slopes(), hypotheses(), and the plotting functions, work with the combined object, and modelsummary() makes tables from it.

Installation and setup 

remotes::install_github("tdmize/suest")
library(suest)
library(marginaleffects)
library(haven)

Basic workflow

Two logit models of union membership, the second adding wages and work experience:

nlsw <- zap_labels(read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/nlsw88.dta"))
nlsw <- nlsw[!is.na(nlsw$union), ]
nlsw[c("collgrad", "south")] <- lapply(nlsw[c("collgrad", "south")], factor)

base <- glm(union ~ collgrad + age + south, family = binomial("logit"),
            data = nlsw)
adjusted <- glm(union ~ collgrad + age + south + wage + ttl_exp,
                family = binomial("logit"), data = nlsw)
combined <- suest(base, adjusted, model_names = c("Base", "Adjusted"))
combined
#> Seemingly Unrelated Estimation
#> Models: Base + Adjusted 
#> Model types: Base=logit, Adjusted=logit 
#> Model engines: Base=stats::glm, Adjusted=stats::glm 
#> Comparison scale: predicted probabilities 
#> Observations: Base=1,878, Adjusted=1,878 
#> Overlapping observations: 1,878 
#> Union observations: 1,878 
#> Parameters: 10

effects <- avg_comparisons(combined, variables = "collgrad", newdata = nlsw)
effects
#> 
#>     Group Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S   2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  Base       0.0966     0.0238 4.07   <0.001 14.4 0.05006  0.143
#>  Adjusted   0.0574     0.0252 2.28   0.0227  5.5 0.00804  0.107
#> 
#> Term: collgrad
#> Type: response
#> Comparison: 1 - 0
hypotheses(effects, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
#> 
#>           Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S  2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  (Base) - (Adjusted)   0.0392    0.00912 4.29   <0.001 15.8 0.0213 0.0571

The last command tests the difference between the two effects directly. That is different from checking whether one effect is statistically significant and the other is not.

Tests on coefficients

hypotheses() lists the coefficients of every model with their joint robust standard errors. b1, b2, … refer to them in that order, so they can be tested against each other across models:

hypotheses(combined)
#> 
#>                   Term Estimate Std. Error      z Pr(>|z|)    S   2.5 %  97.5 %
#>  Base::(Intercept)     -1.33993     0.7041 -1.903   0.0570  4.1 -2.7199  0.0400
#>  Base::collgrad1        0.50691     0.1194  4.246   <0.001 15.5  0.2729  0.7409
#>  Base::age              0.00925     0.0178  0.519   0.6041  0.7 -0.0257  0.0442
#>  Base::south1          -0.74681     0.1161 -6.431   <0.001 32.9 -0.9744 -0.5192
#>  Adjusted::(Intercept) -1.76067     0.7193 -2.448   0.0144  6.1 -3.1705 -0.3508
#>  Adjusted::collgrad1    0.31130     0.1321  2.356   0.0185  5.8  0.0523  0.5703
#>  Adjusted::age          0.00778     0.0182  0.428   0.6684  0.6 -0.0278  0.0434
#>  Adjusted::south1      -0.67692     0.1184 -5.719   <0.001 26.5 -0.9089 -0.4449
#>  Adjusted::wage         0.05384     0.0141  3.820   <0.001 12.9  0.0262  0.0815
#>  Adjusted::ttl_exp      0.00615     0.0131  0.469   0.6387  0.6 -0.0195  0.0318
hypotheses(combined, hypothesis = "b2 = b6")
#> 
#>  Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>       b2=b6    0.196     0.0461 4.24   <0.001 15.5 0.105  0.286
hypotheses(combined, hypothesis = "(b2 - b6) / b2 = 0")
#> 
#>    Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)   S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  (b2-b6)/b2=0    0.386      0.135 2.86  0.00419 7.9 0.122   0.65

Model Fitted with

Zero-inflated Poisson and negative binomial pscl::zeroinfl()
Other GLMs with identity, log, logit, probit, complementary log-log, or log-log links glm(), glm2::glm2()
Tobit regression censReg::censReg(); predictions are the latent mean
Interval, censored, and parametric survival regression survival::survreg() with a common scale
Gompertz and generalized gamma survival flexsurv::flexsurvreg() with dist = "gompertz" or "gengamma"
Truncated regression truncreg::truncreg()

Beta regression betareg::betareg() with a logit, probit, complementary log-log, or log-log link

Bivariate probit GJRM::gjrm(), with the same or different predictors in each equation; mvProbit::mvProbit() with the same predictors

Combining models

Models can use the same, partially overlapping, or completely different samples. Any single-level models can be combined, including models for different outcomes and models for categorical outcomes. Results on different scales are labeled separately rather than treated as directly comparable. Random-effects models (nlme::lme(), pglm(), glmmTMB(), lme4, clmm()) can be combined with each other, including different families, and with linear, binary, count, and ordered models, such as a logit model with a random-intercept logit model. They must share one grouping variable (for three-level models, the top level), which the system is clustered on, and must be unweighted. Random-effects models can have several random slopes and a level nested in the grouping variable. Other panel models (plm(), geeglm()) can be combined only with models of the same kind. Offsets are supported, except in pglm() and glmmTMB() models.

A few models have settings worth knowing about; see Notes on specific models.

Different samples or groups

When the models are fitted to different samples, such as separate groups, use suest_newdata() so each model’s effects are averaged over its own sample:

south_model <- glm(union ~ age + hours + collgrad, family = binomial("logit"),
                   data = nlsw, subset = south == 1)
nonsouth_model <- glm(union ~ age + hours + collgrad, family = binomial("logit"),
                      data = nlsw, subset = south == 0)
fit_groups <- suest(south_model, nonsouth_model,
                    model_names = c("South", "Non-South"))

effects_groups <- avg_comparisons(fit_groups, variables = "collgrad",
                                  newdata = suest_newdata(fit_groups))
effects_groups
#> 
#>      Group Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)    S   2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  South       0.0264     0.0316 0.837    0.402  1.3 -0.0355 0.0883
#>  Non-South   0.1341     0.0335 4.007   <0.001 14.0  0.0685 0.1998
#> 
#> Term: collgrad
#> Type: response
#> Comparison: 1 - 0
hypotheses(effects_groups, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
#> 
#>             Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)   S  2.5 %  97.5 %
#>  (South) - (Non-South)   -0.108      0.046 -2.34   0.0193 5.7 -0.198 -0.0175

Cluster-robust standard errors

Supply a cluster variable to get cluster-robust standard errors for the combined models:

fit_clustered <- suest(base, adjusted, cluster = "person_id")
avg_comparisons(fit_clustered, variables = "x", newdata = dat)

cluster takes one or more column names, or a list with one vector, matrix, or data frame matched to each model’s estimation sample. An observation that appears in more than one model must have the same cluster ID in each. Observations in completely different samples can belong to the same cluster, in which case the covariance between models can be nonzero.

Panel models cluster on the panel identifier by default. A cluster you supply must contain whole panels.

Probability weights

suest supports probability weights for linear, binary logit and probit, Poisson, negative binomial, ordered logit and probit, and multinomial logit models. Fit each model with weights=, and tell suest() that they are probability weights with weight_type = "pweight":

set.seed(376)
weighted <- data.frame(x = rnorm(500), z = rnorm(500))
weighted$mediator <- 0.5 * weighted$x - 0.3 * weighted$z + rnorm(500)
weighted$pw <- exp(0.2 * weighted$z + 0.1 * rnorm(500))
weighted$y <- 1 + 0.7 * weighted$x - 0.4 * weighted$z +
  0.6 * weighted$mediator + rnorm(500)

base_w <- lm(y ~ x + z, weights = pw, data = weighted)
adjusted_w <- lm(y ~ x + z + mediator, weights = pw, data = weighted)
fit_w <- suest(base_w, adjusted_w, model_names = c("Base", "Adjusted"),
               weight_type = "pweight")
fit_w
#> Seemingly Unrelated Estimation
#> Models: Base + Adjusted 
#> Model types: Base=lm, Adjusted=lm 
#> Model engines: Base=stats::lm, Adjusted=stats::lm 
#> Comparison scale: fitted values 
#> Weight type: pweight 
#> Observations: Base=500, Adjusted=500 
#> Overlapping observations: 500 
#> Union observations: 500 
#> Parameters: 9

effects_w <- avg_comparisons(fit_w, variables = "x", newdata = weighted, wts = "pw")
effects_w
#> 
#>     Group Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)     S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  Base        1.003     0.0537 18.7   <0.001 255.9 0.898  1.108
#>  Adjusted    0.722     0.0480 15.0   <0.001 167.3 0.628  0.816
#> 
#> Term: x
#> Type: response
#> Comparison: +1
hypotheses(effects_w, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
#> 
#>           Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  (Base) - (Adjusted)    0.281     0.0322 8.74   <0.001 58.6 0.218  0.345

Weights must be positive and finite. An observation that appears in more than one model must have the same weight in each; weights can differ for observations in only one model, including completely different samples. When the models have different estimation samples, suest_newdata() includes the weights as .suest_weight:

nd_w <- suest_newdata(fit_w)
avg_comparisons(fit_w, variables = "x", newdata = nd_w, wts = ".suest_weight")

Survey data

suest supports the survey models in the table above, fitted from one common one-stage survey design, in any combination:

library(survey)
design <- svydesign(~psu, strata = ~strata, weights = ~w, data = dat)
m1 <- svyglm(yb ~ x, design, family = quasibinomial("logit"))
m2 <- svyglm(yb ~ x + z, design, family = quasibinomial("logit"))
fit <- suest(m1, m2, survey_design = design, observation_id = "id")
avg_slopes(fit, variables = "x", newdata = suest_newdata(fit), wts = ".suest_weight")

If either model uses a subset (domain) of the data, keep design as the full sampled design. The joint covariance accounts for strata, PSUs, and optional one-stage finite population corrections. Replicate weights, multistage designs, calibration, and PPS designs are not supported.

Multiple imputation

To combine results across imputed datasets, fit the same suest system in each one. With mice, with() does this, and marginaleffects functions then estimate within each imputation and pool the results with Rubin’s rules, including cross-model differences:

analyses <- with(imp, suest(
  glm(y ~ x, family = binomial),
  glm(y ~ x + z, family = binomial),
  model_names = c("Base", "Adjusted")
))
avg_comparisons(analyses, variables = "x",
  hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)

mice warns “Large sample assumed.” here. That is expected: SUEST reports large-sample statistics, so the pooled degrees of freedom are Rubin’s large-sample values.

suest_mi() pools the coefficients and their joint covariance:

pooled <- suest_mi(analyses)
summary(pooled)

marginaleffects functions give the same results on pooled as on analyses. A list of suest() results, one per imputation, or the result of with(mitools::imputationList(...), suest(...)) can also be passed to suest_mi(); marginaleffects then warns that it could not recover the original data from a mids object, which does not affect suest() results.
